newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serbs delay ceremony for Bosnian assembly.
newsitem.headline: Serbs delay ceremony for Bosnian assembly.

text.p: Serb leaders baulked at signing loyalty pledges to Bosnia on Saturday and delayed the opening of an inaugural ceremony for the country's new inter-ethnic parliament and collective presidency.

International mediators bargained throughout the day with the Serb member of the presidency, Momcilo Krajisnik, over the ceremonies in which the presidents and deputies were to sign oaths of office symbolising Bosnian statehood.

As guests waited for the ceremony to begin in Sarajevo, Michael Steiner, deputy to the international High Representative to Bosnia, Carl Bildt, discussed the text of the oath with Krajisnik in the Serb government seat of Pale, a mountain village outside Sarajevo.

Moslem and Croat parliament deputies and foreign dignitaries waited in Sarajevo's national theatre but there was no sign of the Serbs by 4 p.m. (1400 GMT), more than two hours after the event was scheduled to begin.
"Krajisnik is playing hardball," said one official in Bildt's office, who asked not to be named.
Bildt indicated as he arrived for the inauguration that the event would go ahead even if the Serb deputies failed to attend.
Asked if the ceremony could take place without the Bosnian Serbs, Bildt said: "Absolutely."
The audience was told at one point that the inauguration would begin shortly and an orchestra began playing music. But the deputies later left the hall.
The 42-member House of Representatives and the three-man collective presidency were chosen in general elections on September 14, nine months after the signing of a peace accord.

Although mediators had won pledges from Serb parliament deputies, the main stumbling block to the ceremony appeared to be Krajisnik -- a hardline Serb nationalist who wants to avoid a public display of support for Bosnia as a unitary state.
Krajisnik said on Friday the venue and the wording of an oath had yet to be agreed and threatened a boycott, Bosnian Serb media reported.
He suggested the meeting take place at Sarajevo airport or the U.S. embassy.
If Krajisnik refused to come to the city centre, there was little that could be done to penalise him, said Colum Murphy, a spokesman for Bildt's office.
"There isn't much we can do. We will do the usual things like send a strong diplomatic protest," Murphy said.
But he said the presidency, which met for the first time on Monday, already exists legally and Saturday's proceedings were merely a "ceremonial" ratification.
"They already have the necessary legal powers."

If the ceremony goes ahead as planned, the three presidents and parliamentary deputies should take the stage and sign a document expressing loyalty to Bosnia and support for the Dayton peace agreement signed last December.

Under terms of the Dayton peace pact, the House of Representives governs a union of Serb and Moslem-Croat territories along with a 15-member upper chamber appointed by regional assemblies, the House of Peoples or Nations.
